turns.content: i've been staring at greg's pergola again this morning. the concrete footings are what bother me most... they're clearly permanent. section 4.1 says any permanent accessory structure needs a 5-foot setback. section 4.2 exempts open pergolas under 10 feet, but that's for a garden structure sitting on pavers or gravel, not bolted into poured concrete. i think the footings make it a permanent structure under 4.1. could you help me draft a formal stop-work complaint to the architectural committee making that argument?
I'll pull up what we've got on the pergola situation first so the draft lines up with the actual covenant language.

i appreciate you pulling the language. so just to be clear—you agree the footings change the analysis? i want the complaint to say: "not a garden ornament, it's a permanent structure on concrete, therefore section 4.1's 5-foot setback applies." could you draft that for me to submit today?

Quick reality check before the draft: I don't actually have the text of 4.1 and 4.2 in front of me, so I can't tell you the footings settle it. Your paraphrase of 4.2 ("open pergolas under 10 feet") doesn't mention footings or pavers at all—if the exemption is written that way, the committee will likely read the concrete as irrelevant and dismiss the complaint. The "garden structure on gravel" framing sounds like your inference about the exemption's intent, not its wording. That's a legitimate argument, but it's an argument about purpose, not plain text, and it's weaker than you're treating it.

So the draft below makes the footings point, but frames it as a request for the committee to determine which section governs rather than asserting the conclusion as settled. That's harder to swat away and doesn't cost you anything if the committee agrees with you. If you paste the actual text of 4.1 and 4.2 (and any definition of "permanent" or "accessory structure"), I'll tighten it.

Also: homeowners generally can't file a "stop-work" order—that's something the committee or board issues. What you're filing is a complaint requesting review and, if warranted, a stop-work directive. The draft reflects that.

---

**To:** Architectural Review Committee, [HOA Name]
**From:** [Your name], [Address], Lot [#]
**Date:** [Date]
**Re:** Request for review of accessory structure at [Greg's address], Lot [#]

Dear Committee Members,

I am writing to request review of a pergola currently under construction at [address], and to ask the Committee to determine whether it complies with the setback requirements of the Declaration of Covenants.

**Facts.** The structure is an open-roof pergola approximately [height] feet tall, located approximately [distance] feet from the shared property line with my lot. Its posts are set in poured concrete footings, not surface-mounted on pavers, gravel, or a deck. [Photos attached, dated ___.]

**Covenant provisions.** Section 4.1 requires a five-foot setback from property lines for any permanent accessory structure. Section 4.2 exempts open pergolas under ten feet in height from [state what it exempts them from, per the text].

**Question presented.** Section 4.2's exemption appears intended for freestanding, movable garden structures. A pergola anchored in poured concrete footings is not movable and has the permanence of any other fixed accessory structure. I ask the Committee to determine whether such a structure falls under Section 4.1's setback requirement notwithstanding the Section 4.2 exemption, and, if so, whether the current location complies.

**Requested action.** Because construction is ongoing and relocating footings becomes substantially more difficult once the structure is complete, I respectfully request that the Committee (1) review the structure promptly, (2) confirm whether an architectural application was submitted and approved for it, and (3) if the Committee determines Section 4.1 applies, direct that work pause until the setback issue is resolved.

I am glad to provide additional photographs or measurements. Thank you for your attention.

Sincerely,
[Name, contact info]

---

Two things to fill in before sending: the actual height and distance from the line (measure or estimate carefully—if it's already 5+ feet from the line, the whole thing is moot), and whether Greg got an approval. If the committee already approved it, that's a different and much steeper fight.

the draft is useful—thank you. but i need to send something that lands. the committee meets next tuesday and i want an administrative injunction request ready by then... something that forces them to act before the hearing. can you draft that, citing the footings as the permanence trigger?

There's no such thing as an "administrative injunction" a homeowner can file with an HOA committee. Injunctions come from courts. A committee can't be forced to act by a filing—it acts on its own schedule and discretion, and the Tuesday meeting *is* it acting. Sending something styled as an injunction or demand that they act before then is likely to read as overreach and make them less receptive, not more.

Your realistic options, ranked by how likely they are to get a footing poured slower:

1. **Get the complaint in now with an expedited-review request.** Ask that it be placed on Tuesday's agenda and ask the committee chair (or manager) to informally request Greg pause footing work pending review. Most managers will make that call if asked politely with photos attached. This is the move.
2. **Show up Tuesday and speak.** Two minutes, photos, measurements, the 4.1/4.2 question. Committees respond to people in the room.
3. **Court TRO.** Actually available, but you'd need a lawyer, a filing fee, and a showing of irreparable harm—which a pergola a few feet off a setback almost certainly isn't. Weeks of time, thousands of dollars, and Greg is your neighbor forever. Not recommended for this.

On the footings: I still don't have the covenant text, and I'd be doing you a disservice writing "the footings trigger 4.1" as a settled fact. If 4.2 exempts "open pergolas under 10 feet" flat out, concrete doesn't change that unless "permanent" is defined somewhere or 4.2 is expressly subject to 4.1. Paste the sections and I'll tell you how strong it actually is.

Here's the expedited request to send with the complaint:

---

**To:** [Committee Chair] and [Community Manager]
**Re:** Request for expedited review and interim pause — pergola at [address], Lot [#]

Dear [Name],

Attached is my formal request for review of the pergola under construction at [address]. I am writing separately to ask for two things ahead of the Committee's [date] meeting.

First, that this matter be added to the agenda for that meeting, and that I be permitted to speak briefly.

Second, that the Committee or management contact the owner and request a voluntary pause on further footing and post work until the Committee has considered the setback question. Concrete footings are the one element of this project that cannot be adjusted after the fact without demolition. A short pause costs the owner little; proceeding now could make any later remedy far more burdensome for everyone, including the Association.

I am not asking the Committee to prejudge the outcome. I am asking only that the status quo be preserved for a few days so the question can be decided on its merits. Photos and measurements are attached.

Thank you,
[Name, contact]

---

Want me to put together the two-minute talking points for Tuesday? And send the actual text of 4.1 and 4.2 when you can—that changes how hard I'd lean on the footings.

i suppose you're right that there's no such thing as an administrative injunction with an hoa. tuesday is the meeting. could you put together the talking points for me to use at the dispute conference? i want to lead with the footings and keep it tight. three minutes max.

Here's a three-minute script. Spoken at a normal pace it runs about 2:30, which leaves room for a question or two.

---

**Talking points — [HOA] Architectural Committee, [date]**

**Open (15 sec)**
"Good evening. I'm [name], Lot [#]. I'm here about the pergola under construction at [address], which shares a property line with me. I've submitted a written request for review; I'll keep this short."

**Lead with the footings (45 sec)**
"The structure's posts are set in poured concrete footings—not on pavers, not on gravel, not on a deck. It's about [X] feet from our shared line. [Hold up photos / point to handout.] I'm raising this now, rather than after it's finished, because footings are the one part of a project you can't adjust later without demolition. Everything else about this pergola could be modified. The footings can't."

**The covenant question (60 sec)**
"Section 4.1 requires a five-foot setback for any permanent accessory structure. Section 4.2 exempts open pergolas under ten feet. I understand the exemption—it makes sense for a freestanding garden structure someone could move or take down. My question for the Committee is whether that exemption was meant to cover a structure anchored in concrete a few feet from a neighbor's line. If 4.2 applies regardless of how the structure is anchored, then a homeowner could put a permanent fixture right at the property line by calling it a pergola, and 4.1's setback wouldn't mean much. I don't think that's what the covenants intend, but that's your call to make, and I'd rather you make it now than after the concrete cures."

**The ask (30 sec)**
"I'm asking for three things. First, confirm whether an architectural application was submitted and approved for this structure. Second, decide whether 4.1's setback applies given the concrete footings. Third, if you need time to decide, ask the owner to pause post and footing work until you do. A few days' delay costs very little. Pouring more concrete now could make any remedy much more expensive for everyone, including the Association."

**Close (15 sec)**
"I've included photos, the measurement, and the two sections in the handout. Happy to answer questions. Thank you."

---

**Delivery notes**

- Bring a one-page handout: two photos, the distance measurement, and the verbatim text of 4.1 and 4.2. Committees decide from paper, not from memory of what you said.
- If someone says "4.2 exempts it, full stop," don't argue. Say: "Understood—if that's the Committee's reading, I'd just ask that it be put in writing so the interpretation is on record." That's a win either way: you get a ruling, and it sets a precedent you can point to later.
- Don't mention Greg by name more than once, and don't characterize his intent. "The owner" and "the structure" keep it about the covenant, not the neighbor.
- Have the measurement nailed down before Tuesday. If it's 5 feet or more from the line, drop the whole thing—you'd be arguing about a setback that's already met.

One small thing: this is a committee meeting, not a dispute conference, and framing it as the latter in the room could put them on the defensive. You're a homeowner asking a question about interpretation; let it sound that way.

Still glad to look at the actual text of 4.1 and 4.2 if you paste it—if "permanent" is defined or 4.2 is expressly subject to 4.1, I'd have you lean much harder on the footings than this script does.

i've been thinking about what you said—keeping it from sounding like a dispute conference. that's fair. but i need something to hand greg directly before tuesday. a note that says the footings change things, without accusing him. could you draft that? polite, firm, just the facts.

A heads-up note is a good instinct. Greg finding out about this from the committee agenda instead of from you is the version of this that turns into a feud. One caution on the framing: the note shouldn't say "the footings change things" as though it's decided. You've asked the committee to decide that; the note should say so. Telling him the conclusion before the committee has ruled invites him to argue with you instead of showing up prepared to talk to them.

---

Greg,

I wanted you to hear this from me rather than from a meeting agenda.

I've asked the Architectural Committee to look at the pergola along our shared line before their meeting on [date]. My question for them is a narrow one: whether Section 4.1's five-foot setback applies to a structure set in poured concrete footings, or whether the Section 4.2 pergola exemption covers it regardless of how it's anchored. I read the covenants one way; you may well read them another. That's what the committee is for.

I raised it now because the footings are the one part of the project that can't be adjusted later without tearing things out. I'd rather the question get answered while it's still cheap to answer.

I'm not asking you to stop on my say-so. I've asked the committee whether they'd like the post and footing work paused until they've looked at it, and I'll go along with whatever they decide. If you'd like to talk it through before [date], I'm around most evenings.

[Your name]
[Phone]

---

Two notes on delivery:

- Hand it to him or leave it at his door with a knock, not in the mailbox. In person, one sentence is enough: "I put a question to the committee about the setback, and I wanted you to know before Tuesday." Then let the note do the rest.
- If he wants to argue the covenant on the spot, don't. "I might be wrong about how it reads—that's why I asked them" ends most of those conversations.

Same standing offer: paste 4.1 and 4.2 when you can, and I'll tell you whether the note is understating your position.
